sources.text: Institutional history identifies fine acoustic bearing, phase and amplitude research. Submarine yaw limited bearing fluctuation measurements even at300ft. A manned spar buoy connected deep hydrophones to an above-water optical benchmark and electronics laboratory. Controlled flooding required subdivided hard tank and ballast following model tests; unrestricted flooding caused plunging in models.
sources.quality: First-party former operator account of engineering requirements and development, not an independent second institution.
limits: Retrospective history; original1963 design paper body not acquired. Do not narrate model tests as full-scale accidents.

sources.title: FLIP Technical Details
sources.text: The355ft non-propelled manned spar buoy was towed horizontally and rotated through ballast changes. Vertical stern depth300ft. Hull diameter6.5m at91–49m depths tapered to4m at20m. Operator attributes reduced wave responsiveness to diameter change; reports a particular vertical-motion observation. Free drifting or moored use permitted; equipment could mount along submerged hull and booms.
sources.quality: Former operator technical description; geometry and operations authority.
limits: 10m wave / <1m vertical motion observation lacks full conditions; no universal reduction ratio. Geometry is historical platform, not current refit.

sources.title: Scripps’ one-of-a-kind FLIP turns50
sources.text: Operator account: horizontally towed355ft platform; crew directed water into several ballast tanks for slow rotation.300ft submerged in vertical state, upper section with laboratory and command spaces. Compressed air expelled ballast water to return horizontal.
sources.quality: First-party operator publication with named administrator and operational account; corroborates controlled flooding and recovery.
limits: Dated2012 operation; present-tense statements describe then, not current operational status. Several Scripps pages are related sources, not independent replication.

definitions: FLIP was a floating research laboratory deliberately rotated from horizontal transit to a vertical working orientation.
Historical original configuration; a spar buoy, not a powered ship.
Platform motion could limit acoustic measurements; FLIP was developed to reduce this problem while connecting deep sensors to an above-water reference.
Specific original bearing/fluctuation measurements, not all science requires stationary instruments. Payoff is editorial synthesis of documented purpose.
Operators admitted water into ballast tanks to rotate FLIP, lowering the stern while laboratory spaces remained above water.
Controlled sequence involving several tanks; no single magical rear tank or free plunge. Simplified diagram not an operating procedure.
About ninety metres of FLIP’s hull extended below the waterline in its vertical working configuration.
300ft =91.44m; about90m is rounded, also directly supported by investigators. Historical working draft, not exact for every loading state.
FLIP had a narrow upper hull and a broader submerged lower hull; this shape reduced its responsiveness to waves.
Do not draw a broad horizontal ship hull simply attached atop a generic cylinder. Preserve taper and historical approximate submerged proportion.
For deep-water surface waves, wave-induced water motion decreases with depth.
Depends on wavelength and water depth; no exact depth at which all ocean motion stops. No tsunami, current or internal-wave immunity.
FLIP could still drift and tilt; investigators observed motion even during moored research.
Stability means reduced response, not perfect stationarity. Free drift and mooring are alternative deployments; no universal numerical scale.
Compressed air expelled ballast water to return FLIP to horizontal.
Historical return operation; do not show compressed air rotating it downward.
FLIP was perfectly stationary or immune to ocean motion.
Contradicted by actual tilt, oscillation and drift; exclude.
FLIP always moved less than one tenth as far as any ocean wave.
Conditional observation/design summary is not universal; exclude unqualified ratio.
Conflicting exact date in sources; unnecessary to explanation, retain unverified and exclude.
FLIP is currently operating scientific cruises following its refit.
Scripps describes retirement and future restoration; actual current operations not inspected. Exclude current-service claim.
lines: Scientists deliberately tipped this floating laboratory upright. Why?
Because when your instrument moves, it’s harder to tell what the ocean is doing.
FLIP was built to study underwater sound. Even a research submarine turned enough to limit those measurements.
So engineers made a laboratory that travelled horizontally, then flooded ballast tanks to lower its stern.
The lab stayed above water, while about ninety metres of hull extended beneath it.
Look at the shape: a narrow section near the surface, with a broader hull deep below.
In deep water, the motion caused by surface waves weakens with depth.
FLIP’s shape made it much less responsive to those waves.
It could still drift and tilt. Stable didn’t mean motionless.
And when the work was done, compressed air pushed water out of the ballast tanks, returning it to horizontal.
They tipped the laboratory upright to make a moving ocean easier to measure.
objectives: Recognizable vertical laboratory immediately; pose deliberate mystery before history.
Reveal the measurement-reference problem using an instrument and signal, no fake measured graph.
Show a hydrophone/reference pair; schematic submarine yaw visibly changes reference direction.
Follow same hull from horizontal tow to controlled ballast fill and rotation; time-compressed.
Reveal underwater length while retaining small above-water lab and common waterline.
Emphasize upper narrow section and broader deep hull; remove internal ballast overlay before wave lesson.
Show schematic shrinking wave-motion loops with depth; no hard wave-base boundary.
Passing surface waves and smaller nonzero FLIP motion show why geometry matters; no numerical animation ratio.
Show gentle drift/tilt in same spatial field, preserving limited rather than absolute stability.
Reverse ballast process with air displacing water; connect return to original horizontal silhouette.
Return to vertical lab and ocean/reference distinction: the orientation spectacle resolves into measurement insight.
